question: HRCT temporal bone of a 35-year-old man with long-standing CSOM and foul-smelling ear discharge shows a non-dependent soft-tissue mass in the attic (epitympanum) with erosion of the scutum and lateral wall of the attic. What is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.text: Granulation tissue — it is the most common soft-tissue finding in CSOM

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Granulation tissue can occur in CSOM but does not typically erode bone. The key differentiating feature of cholesteatoma is its destructive, expansile nature with bone erosion — particularly scutum erosion is the hallmark.

answers.text: Cholesteatoma — non-dependent soft tissue with bone erosion (especially scutum) in the attic is characteristic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cholesteatoma on HRCT appears as non-dependent soft tissue in the attic or middle ear with erosion of the scutum (lateral wall of the attic) and adjacent bony structures. Its expansile, keratinous nature erodes bone — distinguishing it from fluid or granulation.

answers.text: Glomus tympanicum — a vascular tumour that erodes the floor of the middle ear

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Glomus tympanicum is a highly vascular paraganglioma that typically appears as a soft-tissue mass on the cochlear promontory. It does not erode the scutum and would show characteristic vascular enhancement on contrast imaging.

answers.text: Fluid in the middle ear — retained secretions from CSOM fill the attic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Middle-ear fluid is dependent and shifts with position. The key descriptor here is non-dependent soft tissue with bone erosion — a non-dependent position is characteristic of cholesteatoma, not fluid.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the cholesteatoma signature on HRCT: non-dependent soft tissue (moves against gravity) in the attic or middle ear, with erosion of the scutum, ossicles, tegmen, or semicircular canals.

Well done. Non-dependent soft tissue + scutum erosion + attic location = cholesteatoma until proven otherwise. This imaging finding directly determines the surgical approach (canal-wall-down vs. canal-wall-up mastoidectomy).
